#9355. Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create new jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

For example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, says Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” says Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

“If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our plan, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”

Turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

For example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

“Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”

Still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”

To this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

“We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

While her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#9354. The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

#9353. 12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a big conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

Anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act quickly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

Note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are new, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

Anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

This response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

For most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

Try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

Grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

Exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

Try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

If physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

Physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

“Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

Some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re new, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!)

When symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

Anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

These physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re new or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

It’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are new and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

For example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

Breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

#9352. Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. New research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

The new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

The regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

After coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet."

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways."

Materials provided by University College Cork. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9350. Winter workout ideas (plus how to stay motivated all season)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Ah winter. It’s dark out, cold, and there’s a biting wind whistling down the street. Wanna grab your running shoes and start pounding the pavement? We didn’t think so.

When winter hits, it’s no surprise that many of us ditch our workout routines and reach for the hot cocoa instead. And while it’s normal to feel a little unmotivated as the weather shifts, winter exercise doesn’t just help us stay fit, it can help us manage stress and keep our energy levels up. Exercising during the winter can also boost your mood — which can be super important if the cold temps and long nights get you down.

Staying active during the colder months doesn’t have to mean pushing yourself to the max or braving harsh conditions if that’s not your thing. There are plenty of ways to make winter workouts more fun and enjoyable. With a few small adjustments, you could soon start to notice how much better you feel during this time of year.

Winter can feel tough on our bodies and minds, with shorter days, less sunlight, and colder temperatures. These changes can make us feel more tired, sluggish, or even a little down. This is especially true if you get the “winter blues” or seasonal affective disorder (SAD), where the lack of sunlight means your mood and energy levels take a dive. (Currently in a funk? These nine tips can help shift a low mood.)

Exercise can play a big role in managing these wintertime challenges because moving your body can trigger the release of natural mood-boosting chemicals, fight stress and help you to think more clearly.

Getting active in the winter can also improve sleep and help regulate your sleep-wake cycle, so even if you’re feeling thrown off by the longer nights and early darkness, exercise can help you get the rest you need to start your mornings on the right foot. Cue a good mood and steady energy throughout the day too!

Finding the right workouts for winter doesn’t mean you have to head out into the cold — but you can if you want to!

There are so many options you can enjoy indoors—even on the chilliest days—depending on what feels best for you. These are ten great winter workouts that’ll keep your body moving, boost your energy, and help you feel your best.

Ideal for warming up stiff muscles and relieving stress, plus, you don’t need much space or equipment — just a mat or a soft carpet. Check out online classes and videos for beginner to expert workouts.

Use dumbbells, resistance bands, or your body weight — or grab a can of tomatoes from your cupboard! Try exercises like lunges, squats, and push-ups indoors, so you can maintain or build muscle without braving the cold.

If you have access to equipment, enjoy cardio without the cold. These machines let you set a steady pace, so you can up your fitness without overdoing things.

Dancing is great fun, but it’s also a fantastic cardio workout. Try a virtual dance class or follow a YouTube tutorial for a quick, energetic session to get your heart pumping and your face smiling. You can even invite your friends over for an 80s aerobic dance party and dress the part too!

💙 Only have five minutes? Add Mel Mah’s Dance Break to your routine.

If you’re up for some fresh air, bundle up and head out for a winter hike. It’s a great way to explore nature, and the cold will likely feel refreshing once you start moving. Just be sure to dress in layers and check the weather before heading out.

Ice skating might look effortless, but it’s a solid workout for your legs and core. Many local rinks are open during the winter, and even if you’re a beginner, it can help you stay active and try something new. Make it social and see if your coworkers want to join you for a weekly session after work to help keep you motivated.

With the right winter gear, running outside can be invigorating. Layer up in moisture-wicking clothes to keep comfortable, and watch for icy spots to stay safe.

💙 Try Mel Mah’s Mindful Run to experience 20 minutes of running with intention.

If you have snow where you live, give cross-country skiing a try. It’s a full-body workout that’s low impact, making it gentle on the joints and awesome for the eyes. It’s the perfect way to soak in the beautiful scenery and the fresh air of a winter wonderland.

Pilates strengthens core muscles and improves flexibility, and like yoga, it doesn’t need much space or equipment. Follow an online session to get a workout that supports your whole body, or practice some basic moves on your own.

Combine bursts of high-intensity exercise with rest intervals to get a lot of action in a short space of time. These workouts can be easy to do at home and don’t require any equipment, just a little space for a few dynamic moves.

Once you've picked a few workouts, the next hurdle is getting yourself to do them. We get it. These six tips may help you stay motivated and safe while you exercise in colder weather.

Start by setting small, achievable goals that feel right for the season. Winter can be more about maintaining your fitness and feeling good rather than pushing for big gains or intense goals.

Decide on manageable goals like working out three times a week or moving for 20 minutes a day so they feel achievable, and don’t forget to leave room for flexibility.

And when you’re really struggling, aim to just get started. Once you’ve got your sneakers on, you might find it easier to begin that workout. Be gentle with yourself and listen to what feels best for your body and mind — some days might feel easier than others, and that’s completely normal. These seven tips can help you push through a workout mentally.

Decide on a time that suits your energy levels and lifestyle—like in the morning, during lunch, or in the evening—and stay consistent. When you make exercise a regular part of your day, you’re less likely to have to force yourself to do it.

And remember, it’s okay if some days don’t go as planned — just get back to your routine the next day.

If you plan to workout outside, layer up your clothing to stay comfortable and dry as it can make winter exercise much more enjoyable.

Start with a breathable, moisture-wicking base layer, add a mid-layer for insulation, and finish with a wind-proof, waterproof outer for protection from the elements. Add gloves, a hat, and warm socks to keep your fingers and toes cozy and safe, too.

Even if you’re just heading out to a studio down the street, make sure to dress warmly so that once you’re done sweating, you don’t catch a cold.

Cold weather makes muscles tighter, which can increase your risk of injury. To help prevent this, start every workout with a warm-up, especially if you’re outside. Spend 5–10 minutes doing dynamic stretches or gentle movements like walking in place, jumping jacks, or arm circles to get your blood flowing and prepare your muscles.

A good warm-up loosens up your body, reduces stiffness, and gets you ready for the main part of your workout.

When you venture out for your exercise, see if a friend wants to join you so you can catch up while you work out or grab a coffee after a class. The shared experience can boost your mood and keep you going, even on days when it’s tough to get moving.

No real-life takers? Look for online fitness classes, join a virtual exercise challenge, or check if a friend wants to work out “together” by video call. Virtual communities can create accountability, which can help you stick to your goals. And who knows, you might even make a new friend out of it, too!

Staying active in winter deserves a celebration! Treat yourself when you hit small milestones — have a seasonal-spiced herbal tea after a workout, click “buy” on that new piece of workout gear you’ve been eyeing for months now, or become your own DJ and make a fun, feel-good playlist to exercise to.

Rewards can make the experience more enjoyable and give you something to look forward to. Even simple treats, like watching an episode of a favorite show or getting into comfy clothes post-workout, can help you recognize your efforts and build positive vibes around your winter workouts.

It can be tempting to start your outdoor exercise at a sprint because it’s so cold out, but that might risk stiffness and injury in cold muscles.

You’ll need to warm up first, so begin with 5–10 minutes of dynamic movements to gradually increase your heart rate and warm up your muscles.

If stepping out in sub-freezing temperatures to do your gentle movements doesn’t sound appealing (and we don’t blame you,) warm up inside before you head outdoors.

During colder months, there are lots of ways you can stay in shape and boost your mood by getting active:

Whether you venture down the block to the gym or stay at home, these indoor exercises need minimal space and equipment.

It might be chilly, but there’s still joy and beauty in the winter — and exercise options available whether you’re close to nature or city-based. Make sure you’ve got proper gear and choose safe paths.

To prevent winter injuries, a few simple but important steps can help you take care of yourself.

Dress warmly in layered, moisture-wicking clothes to keep muscles warm and flexible. Make sure you warm up with gentle cardio or dynamic stretching to get blood flowing, as cold muscles are prone to strain.

When outdoors, avoid icy or uneven surfaces and use footwear with a good grip for stability. Most importantly, listen to your body — if something feels off, don't push through it. Instead, adapt to your needs and take it day by day.

Strangely, we tend to feel less thirsty in winter, even when we’re losing water during exercise. So stay aware and follow these easy tips to maintain hydration and support your body's performance and recovery.

Keep a water bottle handy and take small sips throughout your workout. You might even set reminders to drink water before, during, and after exercise. Also, if cold water is unappealing, opt for warm drinks like herbal tea or water with lemon to stay hydrated and warm.

If you’re feeling low because of the dark days and winter weather, you can combat winter blues with exercise, even if it’s just a little bit of movement. That’s because getting active can boost your mood and energy by releasing natural feel-good chemicals.

Set yourself a routine to get out for a walk in the fresh air (and sunshine, when the sun shows its face) and gather your friends or family to make it a fun, social occasion, too — which can also help you stay accountable.

Prefer to stay indoors? Counteract shorter days by sitting near a window or using light therapy to lift your mood, and join a virtual fitness class for encouragement and connection. Be kind to yourself — every bit of self-care can help make winter brighter and healthier. (Take a look at these 20 self-care practices for inspo).

#9348. Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide important clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

New research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

"Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," said Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable."

Earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

The Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

"The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," said Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before."

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of New Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

During each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face showed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

The results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an important role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb said.

"We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions."

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb said.

The distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

The researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9347. When is World Meditation Day? Plus, 5 ways to celebrate

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

So many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends. The never-ending to-do lists can wear us down, and any remaining free time we may have is spent zoning out in front of the TV or scrolling on our phones. Taking time to pause, breathe, and connect with ourselves may feel impossible, so sometimes we need an extra push.

World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.

World Meditation Day is held each year on December 21. It’s dedicated to the practice of meditation, a technique that’s been used for centuries to nurture a sense of calm and inner peace. The day is designed to promote awareness about the benefits of meditation and encourage people to bring the practice into their daily lives to restore a sense of balance and clarity.

Originating in India around 1500 B.C., meditation initially combined spirituality with the religious and philosophical life of Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The aim was to cultivate mindfulness and a deep, inward connection to the divine — or the inner self.

Meditation practices spread across Asia and to the Western world, where techniques were adapted to make them relevant to the unique spiritual, therapeutic, and practical needs of each culture.

During World Meditation Day on December 21, people around the world acknowledge and celebrate the rich history and evolution of meditation. The day reminds us of meditation's ancient roots and its wide-ranging health and well-being benefits.

In December 2024, meditation got its own spot on the global calendar when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution proclaiming December 21 as World Meditation Day. The resolution invites people everywhere to observe the day in a way that suits them and to help raise awareness of the benefits of meditation.

Despite a long history, meditation is becoming more and more important in the modern world.

Stress reduction: Regular meditation may help decrease our level of stress hormones, like cortisol, helping to reduce stress and leading to improved mental health and decreased risk of stress-related diseases.

Enhanced concentration: Meditation can help train the brain to focus for longer periods, which can enhance productivity at work. This improved attention span can be extremely beneficial when we’re constantly bombarded with distractions and information.

Promotion of overall well-being: Meditation has been linked with many physical health benefits, including lowered blood pressure, reduced anxiety, and better immune system response.

Contribution to global harmony: By cultivating personal peace and mindfulness, meditation can encourage positive interactions. In this way, World Meditation Day helps promote unity across different cultures and communities.

Whether you’re an experienced meditator or new to the practice, taking part in World Meditation Day can be a fulfilling, enriching experience.

Many organizations host global meditation sessions on World Meditation Day. Connect with thousands of others around the world who are practicing meditation. This can be a powerful experience, emphasizing the unity and collective energy of the human experience.

Seek out workshops, either in-person or online, which can expose you to different meditation techniques and enhance your personal practice.

Plan or attend a group meditation session at a local park, community center, or virtually. Group meditations can help build a sense of community and shared purpose, making the practice more enjoyable and impactful.

If you prefer solitude, dedicate specific time on World Meditation Day for your personal meditation practice. Create a special session where you focus on your intentions, gratitude, or personal peace, allowing you to connect with yourself on a deeper level.

It’s always nice to share the positives in life, so why not spread the love by sharing your meditation experience on social media? Use the hashtag #WorldMeditationDay to join the trend. This can help spread awareness about the day and encourage others to get involved.

Here are a few ways you can enhance and deepen your own meditation practice in honor of World Meditation Day.

If you’re new to meditation or prefer a structured approach, guided meditations can be helpful. An experienced practitioner directs you through spoken instructions, often accompanied by calming music or natural sounds. Try a guided meditation to help you focus, explore different techniques, or maintain meditation discipline.

💙 Add the Daily Calm to your meditation routine, for a new 10-minute guided meditation each day.

Establishing a specific area in your home for meditation can significantly improve the quality of your practice and be a reminder to pause and reconnect with yourself. Make your space quiet, comfortable, and free from distractions. You can even personalize it with items that promote relaxation and peace such as cushions, candles, incense, or soothing artwork.

Explore different styles of meditation to help keep your practice fresh and engaging. Beyond the commonly known mindfulness and transcendental meditation, you might try types like zen, vipassana, or heart-centered meditation, which offer their own benefits.

💙 Dive into Practices: Meditation for Beginners, a 7-day guided meditation series, to expand your practice.

Meditation doesn't always have to be a separate part of your day. Add mindfulness techniques into daily activities like walking, eating, or even during breaks at work to help you stay present throughout the day.

💙 Explore how meditation can be practiced during your 9-5 with the Mindfulness at Work series.

Engaging with fellow meditators can provide support, motivation, and deeper insight into your practice. Look for online forums and local groups that offer meetings, discussions, and shared meditation sessions, which can be particularly enriching.

💙 Join the Daily Calm Community on Facebook to engage with other meditators and share questions and experiences from your practice.

While meditation has been around for centuries, the origin of World Meditation Day isn’t clear. World Meditation Day has been observed for many years and has grown in popularity across the globe in recent years as more people have embraced the practices and recognized their benefits.

We celebrate World Meditation Day to recognize and promote the many benefits of meditation. These benefits can include reducing stress, improving concentration, enhancing emotional health, and building a sense of peace and community. The day encourages new and seasoned meditators to dedicate time to their meditation practices and to positively impact personal and global well-being.

If you’re organizing a meditation event in your community, a few simple steps can help make your event a success.

Start by choosing a suitable location such as a community center, park, or an online platform.

Next, decide on the format of the event — for example, a guided meditation, silent meditation, or a workshop with a knowledgeable instructor.

Promote the event through local community boards, social media, and word of mouth.

Provide clear instructions about what participants should bring (such as mats or cushions) and what they should expect from the event.

There are many virtual meditation resources available to help guide your practice. Explore Calm’s variety of guided meditations, which are suitable for all sorts of different levels and goals, such as stress reduction, better sleep, or increased focus. There’s even a handy beginner series to help you get started, and blog posts on how to meditate if you need a few tips. These resources can make it easy to bring meditation into your daily routine, no matter where in the world you are or how experienced you are.

💙 If you’re new to meditation, try the Mindfulness for Beginners series, a simple 30-day program for anyone looking to build a meditation practice.

#9346. Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI showed the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

One area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which showed higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

Addiction showed a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

The findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions."

This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Plan of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

#9345. Do you work from home? Here's how to stay focused (and sane)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your commute is a 10-step walk from your bedroom to your desk. The coffee's freshly brewed, and you’re still in your pajama pants. For many people, these types of comforts are the benefit of working from home.

But working from home can also bring up challenges that add up over time, such as a lack of boundaries between work and rest and days that feel lonely. Luckily, the habits you build around your workday can help ease both.

Ahead, we’ll cover how to stay focused and connected while working from home, whether you went remote last month or years ago.

Working from home has upsides and downsides, and you may notice both in the same week. On the plus side:

Time and energy back: Without a commute, you may have more time and energy for the rest of your day.

Higher productivity: In a randomized study, employees who worked from home performed about 13% better than those in the office.

Flexibility without a career cost: In a follow-up study, employees who worked from home two days a week performed as well as their in-office coworkers and were promoted as often. They were also less likely to quit.

Risk of isolation: In a large 2026 study in Science, remote work was linked to about a third of the rise in isolation and mental distress.

Blurred boundaries: Without a commute or an office door, your workday can stretch into evenings and weekends.

Higher burnout rates: In a review of 44 studies from the pandemic years, remote workers often reported burnout.

Small changes to your setup can help you get into work mode. Whether you’re building your first home workspace or refreshing one you’ve used for years, these tweaks can make your workday feel smoother.

A dedicated spot: Pick one place to work, such as the corner of a room or one end of the table. Your brain may start to associate that spot with work.

Natural light: Set up near a window if you can. Morning daylight may help you feel alert during the day and sleep better at night. If you don’t have a window, a warm desk lamp paired with a bright overhead light may ease eye strain.

Physical comfort: Choose a supportive seat and raise your screen to eye level, so discomfort doesn’t pull your attention away. A cushion behind your lower back or a firm pillow under you can stand in for a special chair. If sitting for long stretches is hard on your body, switch positions throughout the day or ask your doctor about seating options that fit your needs.

Fewer distractions: Clear your work surface of anything you don’t need for the task at hand. Close extra browser tabs and silence phone notifications, since digital clutter may pull at your focus in the same way physical clutter does.

Sounds for focus: Some people work best in silence, while others prefer instrumental music or ambient sound in the background. In a noisy home, headphones or earplugs can muffle the commotion. If those don’t work for you, a closed door or a “focus time” sign can let the people you live with know you’re concentrating.

💙 Explore how lo-fi music can support your focus.

Working from home takes away some of the structure an office provides, but a solid routine can bring a bit of it back. Here are a few ideas worth trying:

A morning anchor: Pick one or two consistent habits for the first hour of your day, like making coffee or journaling. A familiar rhythm can help you feel grounded before the day’s demands roll in.

A work-mode transition: Without a commute, there’s often little time between rolling out of bed and starting work. Mark the start of your workday with a quick ritual, such as changing out of your loungewear.

Protected focus time: Block a window in your day for your most demanding tasks, ideally when your energy tends to be highest. Share those hours with anyone you live with, so they know when to give you space.

Movement breaks: At home, your day may include less movement than in an office. Use your breaks to stretch or take a short walk.

A clear finish: Set a consistent end time for your workday, and follow it when you can. Mark it with a small closing ritual, like shutting your laptop and tidying your space, so work doesn’t creep into your evening and wear you down.

💙 Build a focus routine that sticks with Calm’s 7 Days of Focus series.

The strain of working from home can sneak up on you, so it helps to have habits that support your well-being along the way. Here are five gentle tips to start.

Small, regular contact tends to help with isolation more than the occasional big effort. Put one social plan on your calendar the way you would a meeting, such as a standing coffee chat with a colleague or a coworking session. On busier days, or if you work on your own, a midday text or a voice note to a friend counts too.

💙 Want more ideas for staying connected? Here’s how to make and keep friends as an adult.

Protect your time away from work. That means no email in bed, whether it’s first thing in the morning or right before sleep. Mute work apps in the evening and tell your team when you’re offline, so no one expects a reply during that time. If your job needs you to stay reachable after hours, allow only urgent messages through.

💙 Wind down from your workday with End of the Day: Leaving Work on Calm.

Step away from your screen to eat, even for a few minutes. If your energy dips, sit near a window or head outside for some fresh air.

A short meditation or a few minutes of breathwork may be a quick way to ease stress.

a focus meditation at the start of your workday

💙 Try Calm’s three-minute Body Scan for a short guided practice.

Every so often, take a moment to check in on your mood and sleep.

feeling flat, even about work you usually enjoy

pulling away from people you normally talk to

If these linger for weeks, consider reaching out to a doctor or mental health professional. Some employers offer free counseling through an employee assistance program. If you’re self-employed, a primary care provider can refer you to options.

Low motivation while working from home is often tied to missing structure. Without coworkers nearby or a set schedule, you may miss the built-in cues an office provides, such as a colleague stopping by your desk to check in. Try building a light routine and dividing work into smaller tasks.

If you don’t have much space, start with one dedicated spot for work, even if it’s just one end of a table. Add decent lighting and a supportive seat, then store your work gear away at the end of the day so the space can feel like yours again.

If you’re a remote worker, you can start a morning routine with one or two small anchor habits before work begins. That could be a gentle stretch or a few pages of a book. Keep it short, and give yourself time to adjust.

It’s normal to feel lonely when you work from home. If you feel disconnected, contact with friends or colleagues may help, even if it’s a quick call or message.

To lower your risk of burnout, aim to set firm boundaries between work and rest. Choose an end time for your work day and take regular breaks. Those limits can help keep your work from spilling into evenings and weekends.

The best way to stay focused over a long day is to work in blocks and take pauses between them. Work on your most demanding tasks when your energy is highest, reduce visible distractions, and listen to instrumental music or ambient sound if it helps you concentrate.

Meditation may ease stress, but evidence that it improves work performance is still limited. Some studies on workplace mindfulness programs suggest they may reduce burnout and improve well-being. Effects on productivity were smaller and less certain. Most of the studies followed people for about three months or less, so less is known about long-term effects.

#9344. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

#9343. This Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Frequent Headaches

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.

The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).
